title: DHSC Abortion Notification Service Alpha Assessment Service

content.content: From: DHSCAssessment date: 19/06/2025Amber review date: 03/09/2026Stage: Alpha reassessmentResult: Green at reassessmentService provider: DHSC
Service description

Under the terms of the Abortion Act 1967 and the Abortion Regulations 1991, medical practitioners have a statutory obligation to notify the Chief Medical Officer (CMO) of every abortion, within 14 days of the procedure, using an HSA4 form. DHSC are responsible for monitoring the Abortion Act and producing statistics on abortions in England and Wales.The Abortion Notification System (ANS) is the digital service provided by DHSC for medical practitioners to enable them to submit their HSA4 forms. Currently it is possible to submit them using 3 channels – paper, API or webform.
Service users
This service is for:● Abortion providers- Registered Doctors- Nurses and midwives- Telehealth call handlers- Medical secretaries and administrators- IT Systems Administrators
● DHSC staff- Public Health Intelligence Analyst- Social Researcher- Data Entry Team- Medical Advisor
● Data Consumers- Healthcare services and research- Policy and politics- Education and academia- Media- Police
Report contents
1. Understand users and their needs
Decision The service was rated green for point 1 of the Standard.
Optional advice to help the service team continually improve the service:
● continue to research and increase the numbers of participants you have spoken to, although it is acknowledged that you have received consistent feedback with your existing participant numbers.
● continue to strive to recruit users, or proxy users, with additional access needs and low digital confidence using methods already identified and investigated during alpha.
2. Solve a whole problem for users
Decision The service was rated green for point 2 of the Standard.
Optional advice to help the service team continually improve the service:
● continue efforts to research with users on mobile or tablet devices
● consider user testing the proposed new service name and researching the discoverability of the new name through internet search engines
● keep on tracking recommendations for potential legislative changes that have potential to improve user experience and processes in future
3. Provide a joined-up experience across all channels
Decision The service was rated green for point 3 of the Standard.
Optional advice to help the service team continually improve the service:
● carefully consider your roadmap for beta to ensure that you are solving the harder problems first across all elements of the service, to de-risk complexity of delivery in later stages
4. Make the service simple to use
Decision The service was rated green for point 4 of the Standard.
Optional advice to help the service team continually improve the service:
● ensure that you follow through in a thorough manner with your tracking metrics, as the panel felt that you had a well-considered set of KPIs

● ensure that your service support includes clearly documented guidance and consistent recommendations for staff who are expected to utilise any new or modified user roles, such as the ‘super-user’ functionality, that are introduced in beta
5. Make sure everyone can use the service
Decision The service was rated green for point 5 of the Standard.
Optional advice to help the service team continually improve the service:

● continue to involve users with access needs and use your new recruitment incentives that you have indicated for beta phase to focus on increasing the number of people from this user group who are involved in testing
● continue prioritising accessibility including carrying out the plan to commission an external accessibility audit during beta
6. Have a multidisciplinary team
Decision The service was rated green for point 6 of the Standard.
Optional advice to help the service team continually improve the service:
● continue to involve policy colleagues closely with the development of the service and if possible, encourage them to observe user research directly
7. Use agile ways of working

DecisionThe service was rated green for point 7 of the Standard.Optional advice to help the service team continually improve the service:● ensure the team has a robust plan to respond or adapt to potential future changes to abortion policy arising from parliament
8. Iterate and improve frequently
DecisionThe service was rated green for point 8 of the Standard.
9. Create a secure service which protects users’ privacy

DecisionThe service was rated green for point 9 of the Standard.Optional advice to help the service team continually improve the service:● continue working closely with DHSC Cyber team● as this is a first within DHSC, record feedback on experiences for future projects.● look at other authentication approaches used within health and government. Contact NHSE to find out what’s used there and any standards or approaches in place● the legacy service has outdated components leading to vulnerabilities. The new service must have a plan to avoid falling back to this post launch● continue to work closely with DHSC Cyber on the Secure By Design self-assessment and other relevant tasks. The panel note that it is important to include this thinking early and continue throughout beta● the alpha includes a strong set of security recommendations, make sure these carry over into beta and are implemented. The timescales for beta are tight with a hard deadline for ending the existing system, be careful that tactical urgency does not cause lapses in best practice approaches.
10. Define what success looks like and publish performance data
DecisionThe service was rated green for point 10 of the Standard.Optional advice to help the service team continually improve the service:
● the team should consider any potential governance gaps carefully and reach out to partner organisations who have a greater digital deliver capability where appropriate

● the methodology for choosing additional KPIs was well reasoned, based on current pain points and NHS priorities such as time spent completing a form by staff. The team should review these throughout beta to ensure they still reflect what success looks like for the service
11. Choose the right tools and technology

Decision The service was rated amber for point 11 of the Standard. During the assessment, we didn’t see evidence of:  ● clear decisions or decision trees for next steps. While a lot has been done to identify pain points and problems within the current service, the decision routes for next steps is not clear. It is good to be flexible in line with findings, but the team is going into beta with a lot of outstanding questions including known DHSC standard approaches

● The team have worked with DHSC IT and Cyber from an early stage to get feedback and guidance, but it was not clear if they are following DHSC standards – largely because this approach is a first within DHSC. Although this may be outside the control of the project team, this does make them trail blazers and presents additional risk ● alignment with NHSE who will be part of DHSC within the next 1-2 years will be. Make sure that any decisions align with NHSE standards and practices as they will be part of the same organisation post launch ● a cloud-first approach. The alpha findings on the existing system outline replacing non-scalable hosting, which has led to poor performance at busy times, with scalable cloud-first hosting● During the assessment, the team said they were looking into on-prem hosting at the DHSC data centre – The DAC. DAC is not currently approved for PII. Changing from cloud to on-prem is out of step with The Technology Code of Practice point 5 - use cloud first and would need strong justification for this approach to gain spend approval.Optional advice to help the service team continually improve the service: ● given the team will be asking the beta supplier to procure infrastructure as a stopgap, anything that they build must be easily portable. Make sure that this lines up with DHSC and NHSE standards and if a tactical, stopgap platform is needed for launch that a migration plan is included in this activity with a path to a strategic solution ● make sure the stopgap approach does not risk exposing the service to poor performance, see related comments under point 14
Reassessment:
The service was rated green after reassessment for point 11 of the Standard.
12. Make new source code open

DecisionThe service was rated green for point 12 of the Standard.GitHub: https://github.com/DataS-DHSC/Abortion-NotificationOptional advice to help the service team continually improve the service:● the team have planned an approach of build over buy as the requirements would lead to heavy customisation of any CoTS product with dependencies on the supplier for compatibility● the team have shown a strong commitment to making things open in alpha. This must continue in beta and suppliers for the current or future phases must agree to this open approach
13. Use and contribute to open standards, common components and patterns

DecisionThe service was rated green for point 13 of the Standard.Optional advice to help the service team continually improve the service:● give feedback on findings on admin and professional patterns which are outside the core public facing design system and have a different, professional, user base● the team have identified what appear to be common pain points such as having to map legacy APIs onto new version. Scanning paper forms may also fall into this category as health and wider government are still using paper forms with need to scan. Although this may be wholly handed over to a 3rd party though directly rather than via another supplier. Make sure these learnings are shared● use the design system in a way that supports easy updates so the service can stay in line with ongoing changes to the design system
14. Operate a reliable service

DecisionThe service was rated green for point 14 of the Standard. Optional advice to help the service team continually improve the service:● the team have thought about hosting options, but a short-term stopgap infrastructure is being considered as a tactical approach to meet launch timescales. Depending on the interim approach, this could lead to launching with a service that doesn’t perform well leading to a negative perception from users that could carry forward in how they see the service. The team have identified slow response times as a pain point and want to avoid fall-back to paper. It is critical that private and early public beta don’t create a negative association around performance and reliability

● make sure the team carefully consider costings relating to service options in beta and live and consider learnings from Alpha and the legacy service● the team should agree an SLA and associated service wrapper at the appropriate time. This should be shared with relevant stakeholders and published in a sensible place
Next Steps
[Amber - alpha] This service can now move into a private beta phase, subject to addressing the amber points within three months' time and DHSC assurance/GDS spend approval if applicable.
To get the service ready to launch on GOV.UK the team needs to:● get a GOV.UK service domain name ● work with the GOV.UK content team on any changes required to GOV.UK content
The service must pass a live assessment before:
● turning off a legacy service● reducing the team’s resources to a ‘business as usual’ level, or● removing the ‘beta’ banner from the service

title: Five insights from our D102 brand refresh

content.content: After 12 years, D102 has launched a refreshed brand identity and website. While the visible changes are clear, we know the real value of any rebrand goes beyond the surface.

As a digital-first creative agency for government, we spend a lot of time helping clients evolve their brands to meet changing audience expectations, channels and behaviours. Going through the process ourselves has reinforced an important truth:

Our brand refresh gave us the opportunity to apply the same principles we use with our clients, from understanding audiences and defining a clear purpose to creating an identity that works across channels.
1. Start where your audience is

Too often, digital is treated as an adaptation of the brand, rather than the main environment it’s designed for. But your audience is unlikely to meet your brand for the first time on a piece of stationery. They’re more likely to encounter it on a phone, a website, or a social media feed.
That’s why digital-first design matters.

When we refreshed our own brand, we considered how every element would work across channels, social content, motion and web experience from the outset. The lesson from this is simple: design for where your audiences are most likely to encounter you.
A brand that is designed to flex, scale and adapt from the outset will be far more resilient as communications channels continue to evolve.
2. Get clear on who you are
A new visual identity needs something solid to stand on.
Before we started refreshing the visual elements of our brand, we took time to understand where we are now and where we want to go next.
Over the past decade, D102 has evolved significantly. Our capabilities have expanded, our services have matured, and the world of public sector communications has changed around us.

The agency we are today isn't the same as the agency we were twelve years ago. That meant our refresh couldn't start with a question about what we wanted to look like. We first needed to ask who we are.

We began with research and insight, using what we learned to define our purpose, vision and the personality we want people to recognise in us. This gave us a clear starting point for everything that followed.
Our advice: before you decide how your brand should look, get clear on what it needs to say about who you are.
3. Colour is strategic, not just creative
Colour is often one of the most emotive and memorable parts of a brand. But the strategic considerations behind colour choice are just as important as the creative ones.

As part of our refresh, we introduced a more accessible colour palette designed to perform consistently across digital and print environments. We also selected a primary colour - Canary yellow - that reflected our personality while remaining appropriate for a government-facing organisation.
For organisations undertaking a rebrand, colour decisions should answer three questions:
The strongest colour strategies balance distinctiveness with practicality.
4. Don’t overlook the power of typography
Typography is often underappreciated during rebranding exercises, yet it can shape how an organisation feels as much as any logo or image.

Our move to the ‘Inter’ typeface was driven by accessibility, usability and personality. Available across platforms and devices, it provides a consistent experience while introducing a more approachable, contemporary tone.

The wider lesson for clients is that typography should work hard. A well-chosen typeface can improve readability and accessibility, strengthen brand recognition, and create stronger consistency across channels.
5. Think in systems, not just logos
One of the most valuable lessons from our own refresh was the importance of developing a flexible and cohesive design system, rather than focusing exclusively on a logo.

For us, this emerged through the evolution of our ‘graphic D’. What began as a shorthand reference for ‘D102’ became a versatile visual device that can frame content, highlight information and create distinctive layouts across different formats.
This approach is increasingly important for organisations managing large volumes of content across multiple channels.
A great question to ask is: what visual tools for our brand exist beyond the logo?

A strong brand system provides designers and communicators with flexible building blocks that can evolve over time while maintaining consistency. This creates greater efficiency and stronger recognition across campaigns, platforms and audiences.
What's next? Looking beyond visual identity
One of the biggest misconceptions about branding is that it ends when the visual identity launches. But visual identity is only one part of a broader brand ecosystem.
Alongside our new look, we've been defining our tone of voice and reviewing our content to ensure that how we communicate aligns with how we present ourselves visually.
For clients embarking on a similar journey, it’s important to remember that a brand is not just what people see - it's everything they experience.
The most effective rebrands bring together strategy, personality, language and design into a coherent whole that helps an organisation communicate with more clarity and more confidence.
While every organisation's branding journey is different, certain principles remain consistent:
We’ve created dozens of brand identities for organisations across government and beyond. To see some of our brand case studies, visit d102.co.uk.
If you’re considering a new visual identity, we can help. Get in touch with our team at hello@design102.co.uk to find out more.

title: What is RSV and who is eligible for the vaccine?

content.content: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a major respiratory virus that is most common over the winter period, typically November to February. Most cases are mild, but RSV can be serious, especially for infants and older adults.

Before the vaccine was introduced, RSV caused around 30,000 hospitalisations of children under 5 in the UK each year, and 20 to 30 infant deaths. It also caused around 9,000 hospitalisations annually in adults over 75, often triggering pneumonia or flare-ups of long-term lung conditions.

The vaccination programme is already making a difference. In 2025-26, England saw 50% fewer infants under 6 months admitted to intensive care with RSV compared with the previous season, as the maternal vaccination programme took full effect. Data also shows a sustained reduction in RSV-related hospital admissions among eligible adults aged 75 to 80.
Who is at risk?

Babies are especially vulnerable because their airways are small and their immunity is still developing. RSV can lead to bronchiolitis, a lung infection causing inflammation, and is most common in infants under one year old. Bronchiolitis differs from bronchitis, which affects people of all ages and causes a mucus-heavy cough. Severe bronchiolitis can require intensive care and can be fatal. More information on bronchiolitis is available on the NHS website.

Older adults, particularly those with lung conditions like chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or a weakened immune system, are also at higher risk of severe RSV infection, which can require hospital admission, cause lasting loss of independence, or even be life-threatening.
How can I protect my baby from RSV?

Vaccination during pregnancy is the best way to protect newborns. It reduces the risk of severe RSV lung infection, such as bronchiolitis, by 80% in a baby's first months of life, significantly lowering the chance of hospital admission.
The vaccine works by boosting the mother's immune system to produce antibodies, which then pass through the placenta to protect the baby from birth.

It's offered from week 28 of pregnancy, usually through maternity services, though GP practices can also provide it. If you haven't been offered the vaccine around the time of your 28-week antenatal appointment, contact your maternity service. Vaccination in week 28, or shortly after, gives the best protection, including for babies born early. Later vaccination still offers some protection and can be given right up until birth if needed.

Babies born very prematurely (before 32 weeks) may need a different form of RSV immunisation, as there may not have been time for the mother to be vaccinated effectively. This also applies to babies with certain heart, breathing or immune conditions. These babies are usually immunised by hospital paediatric teams, either in the neonatal unit or at a follow-up appointment.
What are the symptoms of RSV?

RSV typically causes a cough or cold, wheezing, shortness of breath, tiredness and fever. In babies, symptoms may also include fast, noisy or difficult breathing, fussiness, irritability and reduced feeding. Most cases clear up within 2 to 3 weeks. More details are available on the NHS website.
How long is RSV contagious?

People are most contagious while symptomatic, especially early on, with most transmission occurring within 5 days of symptoms starting. However, infectious virus can sometimes be detected before symptoms appear (1 to 2 days beforehand) and can persist afterwards.

Research suggests that babies and toddlers experiencing their first RSV infection may remain infectious for 2 weeks or more, and may spread the virus more easily than those with prior immunity. People with weakened immune systems may also stay infectious for longer.
These factors make RSV difficult to avoid entirely, which is why vaccination is so important for those eligible.
Who is eligible for the RSV vaccine?
The vaccine is offered to:
Visit the NHS website for full details.
Do I need more than one dose?

Pregnant women should have the vaccine during every pregnancy, to protect each new baby. For older adults, a single dose is expected to offer good protection for several years, and the programme is monitoring how long this protection lasts.
Preventing the spread of RSV

RSV spreads through coughs and sneezes. You can help reduce transmission by covering your mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing, ideally with a tissue or into the crook of your arm, and washing your hands regularly with soap and water.

If you have cold-like symptoms, try to avoid contact with young babies, particularly newborns and premature babies. It's entirely reasonable to ask people with colds to keep their distance from a new baby. Even so, RSV can still be difficult to avoid entirely.
UKHSA's role

The UK Health Security Agency leads national monitoring of RSV activity and evaluates the NHS immunisation programmes protecting infants and older adults. This includes tracking infection rates, hospitalisations and seasonal patterns, and assessing vaccine effectiveness. UKHSA also provides clinical guidance for safe vaccine delivery and supplies scientific evidence to bodies such as the Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation, helping shape government policy on vaccine eligibility.

title: Dragons' Den IP Blog - Series 23 Episode 11

content.content: As the summer holidays come to an end, a new school year begins and the nights start drawing in, this ‘summer girl’ over here can’t help but feel a little blue. So, tonight’s episode of Dragons’ Den was just what I needed to lift my spirits.

I just love a happy ending and there were plenty tonight, as the Dragons invested with their hearts and not just their heads. And as always, there were lots of innovative ideas and intellectual property (IP) innovations to spark my interest.
Playing the IP game

First to enter the Den was Glyn Richards with Fingagolf. It's a miniature game of golf played by placing a plastic golf club onto your finger and hitting the ball around the artificial course in as few moves as possible.
Glyn was asking for £30k in return for a 15% share of his business.
It was no surprise that golf enthusiasts Peter Jones and Steven Bartlett were eager to put the game to the test. Then it was on to the all-important questions.

When Jenna Meek asked Glyn if there were any similar games on the market, he explained that there were other finger-golf games out there, but none of them had an actual golf club that fits onto the finger.
As the Dragons’ eyes lit up at the uniqueness of Glyn’s game, I hoped he had taken steps to protect his idea.
Using our ‘search for a trade mark’ tool, I was soon able to locate a registered trade mark for ‘Fingagolf’, owned by Glyn’s company, Hamnashida Games Ltd.
A trade mark is an essential asset when building a brand as it protects your product or business name from being used by any competitors.

You can register words, sounds, logos, colours, or any combination of these, but there are restrictions. For example, your trade mark cannot describe the goods or services it relates to. Whilst ‘Finger golf’ would be deemed too descriptive, ‘Fingagolf’ is a made up word and has been accepted. However, it is worth noting that all trade mark applications are considered on their own merits.
Designed to a tee

As highlighted earlier, the finger golf club is what makes Glyn’s game stand out, so it is sensible to try and protect that element to prevent others from copying it. It’s reassuring therefore to see that Glyn has several registered designs for his unique golf club, including a right and left-handed version.

A registered design protects the overall visual appearance of something. It can include the physical shape, configuration (how different parts of a design are arranged together), decoration or colour, or even the pattern.
Design registration can last for up to 25 years, although you must renew your designs every 5 years to keep them protected.
You can view all six of Glyn’s registered designs on our designs database by searching ‘Hamnashida Games Ltd’.

Once the Dragons heard about the different add-ons to the game, including different courses and scenery packs, they were all lining up for a shot to go into business with Glyn. After offers from three of the Dragons, Glyn eventually accepted golf mad Peters offer of 30k for 30%. Leaving Peter feeling like he hit ‘a hole in one’.
Designed to make a difference
Sticking with the subject of designs, Sam Mabley came into the Den looking for a 10k investment in exchange for 2% of his business, Yes Friends.

Yes Friends is a range of ethical, sustainable, yet affordable clothing that doesn’t compromise on quality. Made in environmentally friendly factories that pay the garment workers a fair wage, Sam is on a mission to transform the fashion industry.
A quick trade mark search tells me that Sam has protected the business name ‘Yes Friends’ with a registered trade mark, so I was keen to see if he had also registered any of his designs.

Whilst Sam hasn’t formally registered his designs, his creations will still be eligible for unregistered design rights. Unregistered design right is an automatic protection, so you don’t have to apply for it, and the length of protection depends on the type of design you have.

Because the fashion industry is ever changing and evolving, some designers prefer to rely on unregistered design rights as their designs are likely to change quickly and there is not always time to apply for a registered design.

However, there is no official register for these rights, so should you need to prove a design is yours, you will need to provide evidence of when it was created by you. One option could be to get signed and dated copies of your design drawings or photos certified and kept by a solicitor or intellectual property attorney.
The best fit
After a careful examination of Sam’s clothing range, including a sniff test from Deborah Meaden, fashion guru Touker Suleyman was keen to find out more about the manufacturing of the garments.
Thankfully, Sam held his own against the Dragons’ questions and it was soon on to the crucial offer stage.
Without hesitation, sustainability champion Deborah laid her cards on the table and offered Sam double the investment (20k), without upping her stake in the business from the original 2% offered:
Although Touker also went on to make Sam an offer, there was no matching Deborah’s generous proposal and Sam gladly accepted, leaving me all warm and fuzzy inside.

title: Watch: how a White Peak beef farmer uses herbal leys

content.content: When we first started our White Peak herbal leys series, we introduced the project and heard from dairy farmer Rusty Mycock about his experience of integrating herbal leys into his farming system.
We're now publishing the next film in the series, featuring beef farmer James Frost.
A herbal ley is a pasture planted with multiple species, including grasses, legumes and deep-rooting herbs, instead of a single grass variety.

Working with Catchment Sensitive Farming adviser Ben Rodgers, James explains how herbal leys fit into his rotation, from establishment and weed control through to forage quality, soil health and biodiversity.
A herbal ley is a pasture planted with multiple species, including grasses, legumes and deep-rooting herbs, instead of a single grass variety.

When implemented successfully, herbal leys can be a major tool in enhancing farm resilience to weather extremes. Like the rest of the series, the film focusses on practical experience and in this case, lessons learned from over 10 years of management within a commercial beef system.

James farms 220 acres in the Derbyshire White Peak, rearing and finishing beef cattle.
In this film he explains his move from dairy to beef production and how a resilient, low input but productive system has evolved around the large-scale use of herbal leys.

title: Leading the way in Greater Manchester – bringing people, nature, connectivity and growth together

content.content: Lucy Abram, Deputy Director of the Cheshire, Lancashire, Greater Manchester and Merseyside Team

CyanLines is a bold plan to link and transform Greater Manchester’s green and blue spaces - and it's just celebrated its first birthday. This blog explores how Greater Manchester is putting nature at the heart of its future growth and development, and celebrates the first year of CyanLines, an ambitious programme connecting people with nature across the city region. It explains the ways in which the city regards nature as essential infrastructure, delivering benefits that range from cleaner air and reduced flood risk to improved health, wellbeing and economic prosperity.
Greater Manchester has long been a leader in reconnecting people with nature. Nature is not a nice-to-have or an afterthought. It is essential infrastructure.

Natural England has been working across Greater Manchester for many years, building strong partnerships with the Greater Manchester Combined Authority, local authorities and environmental NGOs. Together, we are shaping strategic plans and delivering projects that create lasting benefits for communities, nature and the local economy.

Nature cleans our air and water, reduces flood risk, stores carbon, cools our urban environments, supports food production and strengthens the economy. And importantly, access to green space improves physical and mental wellbeing, with green spaces estimated to save the NHS £2.1 billion every year by helping people live healthier lives.
Ensuring these spaces are accessible, with routes starting on people's doorsteps, is more important than ever.

As the first area in the North of England to publish the Local Nature Recovery Strategy, Greater Manchester is leading the way in working across a range of partnerships to integrate nature into the fabric of the city region. This vision goes hand-in-hand with ambitious plans for housing, world-class employment spaces, and hubs for innovation, science and technology, demonstrating that growth and nature are not competing priorities.

The development of CyanLines is a powerful example of this ambition. By creating a connected network of nature-rich spaces linked by walking routes, canals and rivers, the project will make it easier than ever for people to experience and enjoy nature across the city.
It's ambitious. It's transformative. And if there's one thing Manchester has never been afraid of, it is thinking big.
Celebrating One Year of CyanLines

In September 2025, more than 600 people descended upon Aviva Studios in central Manchester to hear of a new ambitious programme that was set to transform the green and blue routes across Greater Manchester. 12-months on, crowds returned to the creative hub on the banks of the River Irwell to hear first-hand of the progress made.

Born from the minds of Tom Bloxham CBE MBE (Chair and Founder of Urban Splash) and Pete Swift (Founding Director and CEO of Planit) – and backed by the former leader of Manchester City Council and recently elected Mayor of Greater Manchester, Bev Craig, and our new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham – CyanLines is a bold initiative to create a 100-mile network of green spaces and waterways across the city region, connecting local people with the nature-rich landscape that makes Greater Manchester so unique.
Mayor of Greater Manchester and co-chair of CyanLines Bev Craig said:

It is part of one of the first projects to be part funded by the Nature Towns and Cities initiative, a transformative coalition of organisations bringing nature, green infrastructure and natural heritage into communities. Salford & Manchester are one area where nearly £1 million has been awarded to create thriving nature corridors and parks to connect existing open spaces and waterways into a cohesive network.

One of the core components of CyanLines is a commitment to be led by the evidence. The CyanLabs programme pulls together key organisations – such as Natural England and academics from Greater Manchester’s Universities – to design where the next tranche of CyanLines should go, to improve nature’s recovery whilst creating more green corridors in areas of most need for the greatest health benefits.

This week, the CyanLines coalition reconnected for the 2026 annual stakeholder event, using the one-year anniversary as a moment to celebrate the development of the four initial routes across the urban centre of Manchester and Salford. A warm reception was received from both private and public partners, celebrating this next phase and revealing two major announcements: firstly, a significant charitable grant from the Bupa Foundation to the National Trust towards Phase Two of Castlefield Viaduct. Secondly, plans for a new CyanLines route, CL5, which will significantly improve the experience of walking and wheeling to the Etihad Stadium and Co-op Live Arena from the City Centre through a series practical and nature led interventions.

As ever, it was striking to see the breadth of representation in the room; from developers who are reshaping areas of Greater Manchester to policy professionals, everyone has united under the CyanLines plan to help deliver for nature and people.

title: How Southwark Council used Get help buying for schools to transform catering procurement

content.content: An innovative collaboration with the Department for Education’s (DfE) Get help buying for schools (GHBS) service helped Southwark Council to set up its own bespoke school catering services framework — one that is already attracting wider interest across London.
The challenge

With funding from the Greater London Authority to pay for school meals, borough chiefs wanted better oversight, to ensure money was being spent wisely and catering services were aligned with the authority’s school meals transformation programme.

“We had the funding commitment from the council, but we didn't have a local authority caterer so our oversight of what was being served in schools was very arm's length,” said Gillian Boundy, Senior Public Health Programme Manager at Southwark Council.
“So, part of the aim was to try to get a little bit more oversight into what was on the plates and thinking about what levers we could use as a local authority to improve quality and value for money.

"The individuals in schools who are making quite sizeable procurement decisions - a school food contract can be £600,000 in a small primary school - don't necessarily have the capacity and knowledge that it takes to do it properly. The supplier bargaining power and the buyer bargaining power, it's off."
A borough-wide solution

As part of its transformation programme the council ran training for school business managers to help them procure catering services more effectively. GHBS was one of the tools promoted to support that.

When school business managers started using the service, GHBS triage staff began reaching out to Gillian for help completing school specifications and it quickly became apparent that a borough-wide approach would be better.

“It became quite clear that it would be more efficient if there was a one-size-fits-all specification and terms and conditions,” said Gillian. “What had been an ambition to create a centralised contract for Southwark actually came to be a bespoke framework agreement with procurement support for school business managers."
Specialist support every step of the way
From that point, GHBS worked closely with the council over an 18-month period - first to tender the framework agreement itself, then to support individual schools.

"We were very grateful for the specialist procurement support from the GHBS team in doing that framework,” said Gillian. “We knew what specification we wanted but we weren't experts in the Public Contract Regulations (PCR) 2015 and they really held our hands through that process. The team have been incredibly supportive.
"Just the flexibility in the service to even consider working at borough level was fantastic. It's really been a very collaborative relationship."
What the framework delivers

Launched in August 2025, the framework gives Southwark Council eight approved catering providers, offering genuine choice - from large national caterers suited to secondary schools, through to smaller providers with a stronger focus on provenance and local produce.

“It allows the schools to retain autonomy over their supplier and some choice around their specific school characteristics and which service they want to offer but also gives the local authority oversight of the service specification, the contract monitoring, the supplier pricing and menus,” said Gillian.

Critically, the framework delivers transparency on pricing. Rather than schools facing a single price per plate with hidden additional charges and unexplained annual increases, it introduces a profit and loss model with guarantees, making costs for food, staffing, management fees and disposables clearly visible.

The framework also reflects Southwark's wider social value priorities. It requires suppliers to pay the London Living Wage and includes commitments on carbon reduction planning, food waste management, employment of care leavers and apprenticeships, and potential support for holiday food and fun clubs.
Early signs of success

The framework is still in its early stages, with one school having completed a successful call-off and five more currently in the tender process. But the reaction has been telling. When Gillian announced it at a school business managers' meeting, she recalled: "Everybody who had to tender started clapping and cheering.

“We suspect our framework will be more useful to small schools that don't have the big procurement functions behind an academy. We're thinking about our maintained schools, our faith schools, who need some support through that procurement system.”

Gillian is already sharing Southwark's experience with other London boroughs and there has been interest from Greater London Authority's policy team around whether the model could be adapted for a city-wide framework.
"Get Help Buying for Schools gives some comfort to people who've been asked to do things who haven't necessarily got the skills. I think it's a win-win,” she said.
“I've learned a lot. Should we do this again, I'd feel more confident tendering a framework agreement. I've certainly benefited a lot from the help, and I think the council's learned a lot.
“The GHBS team have all been very professional and incredibly flexible, paid great attention to detail - and have educated me along the way.”
Find out more about how the Get Help Buying for Schools team can support your school catering procurement.

Any savings, benefits and outcomes described in this case study were provided by Southwark Council and reflect its specific experience and circumstances. Individual results will vary between schools and trusts.

title: An Online Hub for Local Wildlife Sites: New Resources for a Vital 5% of England

content.content: By Sofía Muñoz and Scott Mitchell, Senior Specialists for Data Engagement and Analysis, Natural Capital and Ecosystem Assessment Programme
This blog explains what Local Wildlife Sites (LWS) are, why they matter, and the importance of the new online hub where people can go for information about their own LWSs.

It's not only our best-known landscapes which matter for nature. Alongside designated areas like National Parks and Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs), there's a vast and often overlooked network of 44,000 places across England that matter for wildlife and for people: Local Wildlife Sites. But while Local Wildlife Sites (LWSs) are often well-known and valued locally, their potential to support nature recovery hasn't always been visible at a regional and national scale.

Today, the Wildlife Trusts are publishing a new online hub for LWSs, the result of an ambitious partnership with Natural England, made possible by funding from the UK government’s Natural Capital and Ecosystem Assessment programme. The hub brings together information from across the country to create a national picture, helping communities, planners, and policy-makers understand more about these sites.
What LWSs do for us

LWSs don't carry the statutory protection of designations like SSSIs, but their contribution to nature and to people is significant. They’re identified at a local level by the people who know their areas best, and are selected for biodiversity and nature conservation value. Found on both public and private land, they can act as stepping stones and refuges for wildlife, help connect fragmented habitats, and provide valuable ecosystem services, from flood protection to cleaner air. Where they are accessible, they provide places for people to connect with the natural world.
A national landing page for LWSs

The hub will serve as a national landing page for LWSs. It will raise awareness of these sites and their importance, provide accessible information to the public and existing LWS stakeholders, and signpost users to their relevant Local Wildlife Site partnership or Local Environmental Records Centre (LERC).

It also includes maps of the number and total area covered by LWSs , assembled by the Wildlife Trusts using information shared by LWS partnerships across the country. These show that LWSs cover over 750,000 hectares – over six times the area covered by National Nature Reserves, and approaching the 1,000,000+ ha covered by Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs).
Alongside the new hub, we've also updated the guidance on local sites (Local Wildlife Sites and Local Geological Sites) and best practice for selecting and managing sites.
How will the hub be used?
The hub will support local communities to learn about and care for these sites, better understand their value, and discover and enjoy those of them which are open to the public.

Having this evidence in one place will make it easier for LWSs to be considered in policy development at multiple scales, such as within 30by30, Local Nature Recovery Strategies, and land use planning and decision-making.
An uneven national patchwork

One of the most striking things that this work illuminates is just how differently LWSs are distributed in different parts of the country. These regional differences will have implications for nature recovery. LWSs may be particularly important in an area where protected legal categories are sparse. In Birmingham and the Black Country, for example, although under 2% of the area is covered by SSSIs (against an average of 8% for England), a further 6.8% is covered by LWSs.

In Wiltshire, meanwhile, according to figures from the Wildlife Trusts, 75% of the county’s deciduous woodland is found in LWSs, compared with just 10% in SSSIs. While not all LWSs are in favourable condition or positive conservation management, LWSs can be of equal or higher biodiversity value than SSSIs.
Built on partnership

This work would not have been possible without the many LWS partnerships across England who have spent years, in some cases decades, gathering and maintaining local evidence. We're enormously grateful to them, and to the local custodians of these sites, for their expertise and dedication.

The project was funded through the UK government's Natural Capital and Ecosystem Assessment programme (NCEA), Defra's largest research and development programme. NCEA is assessing England's land, freshwater and coastal ecosystems to produce a baseline of our natural assets by 2029, enabling a natural capital approach to policy and decision-making.

title: Speaking up about mental health in forestry and arboriculture

content.content: Mental health in forestry and arboriculture has, for a long time, been difficult to talk about. It’s a subject that hasn’t had the evidence or data behind it to help the sector understand its scale, or to know where to focus support.
Through this blog I will share findings from the sector’s first survey into workers’ mental health and how the Wellbeing in Forestry group is turning that evidence into action.
A hidden issue in forestry

Office of National Statistics (2024) data shows that men in their early fifties have a higher rate of suicide than other groups. This demographic makes up a large proportion of our forestry workforce: the people who manage our woodlands, care for our trees, and work at the front line of the sector’s contribution to climate change and sustainability.

It’s this gap in understanding, and a shared sense that things need to change, that led to the creation of the Wellbeing in Forestry group in 2024. Supported by the Forestry Commission, this group brought together organisations from across the sector to begin addressing the mental health and wellbeing challenges facing forestry and arboriculture workers. We didn’t know where to start, we didn’t really know how to help but we came together because we needed things to change.
Breaking Points survey findings

To better understand the nature and scale of the mental health challenges in forestry, we conducted a survey of people who work with (or have worked with) trees. The response to this Breaking Points survey was significant with 538 people responding and the findings pointed to a workforce under pressure. The report found:

A particularly concerning figure was that less than half (only 43%) of respondents said they had someone they trusted to talk to on a weekly basis, and 31% said they had no regular or reliable support at all. The report also highlighted lack of respect, lack of understanding and verbal abuse from the public as causes of worry, anxiety and, ultimately, poor mental health.

The survey responses were clear: stress is widespread, deeply felt and often unspoken in the forestry sector. But there is a strong appetite for change. Forestry workers want interventions that reflect their realities and are tailored, accessible and grounded in respect.
A cycle that's hard to break

What became clear when analysing the Breaking Points survey data was how these pressures feed each other. Financial strain pushes people to take on more risk to make ends meet. Isolation means there's often no one nearby to notice when someone's struggling or to share the load with.

A culture that treats stress as something you just get on with makes it harder still to speak up. Phrases like “everybody’s tired”, “don’t complain”, “you are lucky to have a job” and “you’ll get through, you always do” are common, but they can do real harm.

Self-employed workers and machine operators reported the highest levels of isolation, often working solo for long stretches. Arborists reported the highest rates of both safety risk and emotional strain, driven by high-stakes physical work with little recognition.
Managers carried a different weight, such as budget pressure and bureaucracy, alongside the emotional cost of supporting struggling teams while getting little support themselves.
Raising awareness

To mark World Suicide Prevention Day, the RFS released an animation on behalf of the Wellbeing in Forestry group, depicting the challenges and pressures faced by forestry contractors. The aim of the ‘Every Interaction Matters’ video is to foster greater understanding for the everyday struggles of those working on the ground, and that a shift in tone and greater compassion can go a long way.
Building understanding together

Another thread running through the survey is how forestry and arboriculture work is often misunderstood by the public. Felling, thinning and deer and squirrel control are all essential parts of good woodland management, but without context, these activities can look alarming to people who care about their local green spaces. Respondents said they were sometimes met with concern or frustrations from passers-by unfamiliar with the reasons behind the work.

At this year’s Royal Welsh Show, the Royal Forestry Society released a new animation exploring this topic. It depicts a forestry contractor tasked with felling diseased trees to make room for a resilient new woodland, who faces criticism from the local community unaware of the purpose behind the work.
That reaction often comes from a well-meaning place and communities taking an interest in their local woodlands should be welcomed.

The animation encourages people to approach foresters with curiosity when they see forestry operations nearby and to ask foresters what's being done and why, to understand the work that is being carried out. In most cases, it's work that benefits both the woodland and the people who live near it, as a well-managed woodland delivers far more benefits to people, nature, the economy and wider environment.
Future plans to support the sector
The Wellbeing in Forestry group was established to bring a cross-sector response to these challenges.

The Breaking Points survey is itself a direct output through this collaboration, providing the first substantive evidence based on mental health stressors in the forestry and arboriculture sector, giving the group a foundation to target support where it’s needed most.

The group is now developing a toolkit. This toolkit is designed to improve how forestry consultants and contractors communicate, with the aim to reduce the financial and emotional pressure the survey uncovered.

More tools, events and sector conversations are planned over the coming months, including events like APF, the UK’s largest forestry, woodland, arboriculture, firewood, fencing, trees and timber trade show. Grassroots initiatives have also got off the ground in the last year, including numerous ‘Pie & Pints’ events where foresters and arborists meet to talk openly and form connections.
Take action

This World Suicide Prevention Day, we can all take one step to help address these issues by having an honest conversation with a colleague this week. Ask how they’re really doing and see where the conversation leads.

If you would like to share any ideas on how the sector could tackle the issues discussed and highlighted in this survey, the Wellbeing in Forestry group would like to hear from you. Please email Christopher Williams or Jen Turner from the RFS.

This work is part of a wider effort by the Wellbeing in Forestry group, which brings together the RFS, Confederation of Forest Industries, the Forestry Contracting Association, Forest Industry Safety Accord, the Institute of Chartered Foresters, Royal Agricultural Benevolent Institution, the Royal Scottish Forestry Society, the Small Woods Association and the Forestry Commission, working together, to improve wellbeing across the sector.

title: Giving the River Rib room to breathe: restoring a Hertfordshire chalk stream

content.content: Some of England's most special rivers flow almost unnoticed through our countryside. Chalk streams are among the rarest freshwater habitats on Earth, with around 85% of the world's 280 chalk streams found in England.

These rivers are renowned for their crystal-clear waters, rich wildlife and cultural heritage. Yet many have been heavily modified over generations, leaving them disconnected from their natural processes and struggling to support healthy ecosystems.

This summer, we worked in partnership with the Wild Trout Trust, Affinity Water and local landowner Jeffrey Pearman to undertake a major restoration project on a one-kilometre stretch of the River Rib at Latchford, near Standon in Hertfordshire, to help return a section of this precious chalk stream to a more natural condition.
A river shaped by the past
Like many rivers across England, this stretch of the River Rib has been altered by decades of dredging, straightening and neighbouring agricultural land use.

Over time, these changes deepened the river, removed important gravel habitats and disconnected the channel from its floodplain. Natural processes that once maintained a healthy and diverse river environment were lost, contributing to the ‘moderate’ ecological condition of the waterbody under the 2025 Water Framework Directive classification.
Thinking bigger
What made this project particularly exciting was the opportunity to think beyond the existing river channel.

The landowner, Jeffrey Pearman, was willing to dedicate additional land to the project, allowing us to create a more ambitious restoration than would otherwise have been possible. Rather than simply modifying the existing channel, the team was able to create approximately 300 metres of ‘re-wiggled’ river channel and reconnect the river to its wider floodplain.
This approach gives the river more space to move through the landscape naturally, helping it respond to both high and low flow conditions while creating valuable habitat for wildlife.

The approach reflects the principles of the Chalk Stream Restoration Strategy, which promotes restoring natural river processes and reconnecting rivers with their floodplains to improve the long-term health and resilience of chalk stream catchments.
Rob Mungovan, Project Manager at the Wild Trout Trust, said:

"Chalk streams are incredibly special habitats, and projects like this are about giving rivers the space and natural features they need to function properly. Jeff's ambition as a landowner allowed us to push what was possible here. Rather than being constrained by the existing channel, we were able to create something much more ambitious for the River Rib and the wildlife that depends on it."
Restoring natural processes
The restoration works were delivered by Aquamaintain and overseen by the Wild Trout Trust, with support from the Environment Agency and Affinity Water.
The project included:

An unexpected but beneficial aspect of the project was the discovery of substantial quantities of gravel during excavation works. Some of this material was processed and reused on site, helping recreate the riverbed conditions required by native chalk stream species.
Benefits for wildlife
Healthy chalk streams support an extraordinary range of plants and animals.

The restoration will improve habitat for fish species including brown trout, while also benefiting aquatic plants, invertebrates and a wide variety of wetland wildlife. The creation of new wetland habitats and improved floodplain connectivity is expected to provide new opportunities for species such as water voles, otters, wading birds and insects.
By restoring natural river processes, we are not only improving conditions within the channel itself but helping to recover ecological connections across the wider landscape.
Partnership in action
Projects of this scale simply cannot happen without strong partnerships.

The Environment Agency provided funding through the Chalk Partnership Fund and Water Environment Improvement Fund. The Wild Trout Trust led on project development and delivery, while Affinity Water provided support and funding through its ambitious River Restoration programme as part of its wider environmental commitments to protect chalk stream catchments, enhance biodiversity and improve water quality, helping to leave the environment in a measurably improved state. The success of the project also relied on the enthusiasm and commitment of the landowner, who not only made his land available for the restoration works but also provided practical support to Aquamaintain throughout project delivery.
The project demonstrates what can be achieved when organisations bring together their expertise, resources and shared commitment to improving the environment.
George Horne, Senior River Restoration Project Manager at Affinity Water, said:

"This project shows what can be achieved when landowners, environmental organisations and water companies bring their different expertise together around a shared ambition for our chalk streams. Creating more space for the River Rib and restoring the features it would naturally have helps create a healthier environment for wildlife and forms part of the wider work needed to protect these precious habitats for the future."
Looking ahead
While construction has now been completed, the story of the River Rib restoration is only just beginning.

Extensive seeding and tree planting is planned, which will help transform the currently exposed riverbanks, with wetter weather helping vegetation to establish and stabilise the banks alongside ongoing monitoring to understand how the river responds over time. The site will also provide valuable lessons for future chalk stream restoration projects across Hertfordshire and beyond.

Our ambition is that the River Rib becomes an example of how working with natural processes can help restore England's globally rare chalk streams, improve resilience to climate change and create thriving environments for people and wildlife. In doing so, the project supports the Environment Agency's EA2030 ambitions for healthy air, land and water supporting nature's recovery, and for creating a nation that is more resilient to climate change.
By giving the river room to breathe once again, we are helping to secure a healthier future for this special ecosystem.

title: Who’s eligible for the 2026 COVID-19 vaccine, or ‘Autumn Booster’?

content.content: When autumn comes, protection from any earlier COVID-19 vaccination you may have had will be starting to wane. For those who are more likely to become seriously ill from COVID-19, the NHS offers a free vaccine in the autumn, previously known as the 'Autumn Booster'.

Current vaccines provide good protection against severe disease and hospitalisation. UKHSA surveillance data relating to last autumn's programme shows that vaccine effectiveness was 47% for the 3 months following vaccination.

Vaccination continues to help protect against severe illness, hospitalisations and deaths arising from COVID-19. NHS England data suggests that between October 2025 and January 2026 around 16,000 people were admitted to hospital with the virus.
Eligible groups for autumn 2026

Ministers have accepted the advice of the Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation (JCVI) for the autumn 2026 COVID-19 vaccination programme, which focuses on vaccinating those at highest risk of serious disease.
For autumn 2026, COVID-19 vaccination is offered to:
The eligibility is the same across the 4 nations of the UK (England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland).

The vaccine should usually be offered no earlier than around 6 months after the last vaccine dose. If you are eligible, you can get protection from an autumn COVID-19 vaccination even if you have not taken up a COVID-19 vaccine offer in the past.
Eligibility for the immunosuppressed

We understand that having a weakened immune system (immunosuppression) is a lot less straightforward than the other criteria. Looking online can cause even more confusion, as people might see themselves (and be considered by others) as immunosuppressed but might not fit the immunosuppression criteria for vaccination.

So, what are the immunosuppression criteria? Eligibility is outlined in the COVID-19 Green Book chapter, a document published by UKHSA specifically for public health professionals. It can be a complicated document for non-experts, so we've listed some of the groups here:
While this list summarises some major groups, it does not cover everything. Please talk to your healthcare professional if you are unsure.
How to access the COVID-19 autumn vaccination
COVID-19 spreads more easily in winter because we spend more time indoors with others.

Booking for the COVID-19 vaccination is now open. Visit the NHS website and choose a date and time from 1 October. If you are eligible, having your COVID-19 vaccination this autumn will give you protection from serious COVID illness over winter.

title: Making graph databases more accessible with AI

content.content: The bottleneck between questions and answers

Graph databases are designed to store and analyse relationships between connected pieces of data. Analysts working with graph databases often know exactly what question they want answered, but not how to write the query needed to get that answer. A seemingly simple question such as "How does this product move through Company X's supply chain?" can require a complex Cypher query involving multiple connected suppliers, products and routes.

This challenge was raised to us by colleagues in the Global Supply Chains Intelligence Programme (GSCIP). This is a platform that brings together large-scale data to help government understand global supply chains.

While GSCIP analysts need quick access to answers from graph data, many do not use Cypher day-to-day. As a result, data scientists often spend significant time translating business questions into database queries. This can create a bottleneck between the people who understand the problem and the people who understand the database.

To explore whether AI could help bridge this gap, we built a proof of concept (PoC) that translates plain English into graph database queries. Our goal was simple: find out if this approach is feasible and understand the trade-offs involved. This would help to inform us about how AI could reduce pressure on specialist teams, and what guardrails would be needed in a live environment.
The experiment
Our lightweight proof of concept was designed for rapid experimentation.

At a high level, the system allows a user to ask a question in plain English, such as "Which organisations are connected to this project?" and automatically converts that question into a database query. The system then retrieves the relevant information from a graph database and returns the results.

To keep the design flexible, we exposed the capability through a simple interface that could be integrated with other tools and tested against a range of example questions. This allowed us to focus on the core challenge: reliably translating natural language into queries that can navigate complex relationships in graph data.

For readers interested in the technical implementation, the solution was built using a graph database and a text-to-query component that generates Cypher queries from natural language, as shown in Figure 1.
Synthetic data supporting AI development and testing
To support development and testing, we built a synthetic data generator capable of producing graph data matching the data structure and size we would expect in a real environment.
This allowed us to generate realistic test data and quickly load it into the platform through an API, without exceeding the capacity of our local systems.
Using synthetic data gave us more flexibility in the testing process and minimised the need to process real data.
How can we be sure it works?

Before releasing the tool to analysts, we needed a robust way to assess the reliability of its generated queries. We used DeepEval, which is an evaluation framework for Large Language Models (LLMs), to evaluate query quality and performance.

We also recognised the limitations of using LLMs to evaluate LLMs (LLM-as-a-judge), as is done with DeepEval. To mitigate this, we complemented automated evaluation with targeted human reviews, helping us better understand failure modes and measure true accuracy.
What we learned: a correct query is not always the right query

While the experiment was not intended to benchmark production-level accuracy, it demonstrated that natural language questions could be translated into executable graph queries across a range of test scenarios. This gave us confidence that the approach was feasible.

One of the most important findings was that generating syntactically valid, runnable queries is not the hardest problem. The greater challenge is ensuring that each query genuinely reflects the user's intent. As a result, the same question can sometimes produce different answers depending on how that intent is interpreted.

This has important implications for anyone looking to build on or replicate this work: evaluation cannot focus solely on query correctness but must also assess whether the generated query captures the intended meaning of the original request. This increases the need for careful testing.
A spectrum of approaches
One of the key questions for this experiment was understanding what kind of approach is even feasible. In practice, translating natural language into graph queries sits on a spectrum:

The experiment highlighted a trade-off between flexibility and consistency. Fully generative approaches are more flexible, but produce less consistent results. Deterministic approaches offer greater reliability, but narrower coverage. Our testing suggested that a hybrid approach may offer the most practical balance between the two. A deterministic query bank can handle common, well-understood questions, while LLM generation is reserved for unusual or more complex questions. This shifts effort away from continuous runtime validation toward upfront verification of trusted query patterns.
Benefits of our work

This work did more than test whether the technology could work. It gave us a clearer understanding of how we could make graph data more accessible to analysts. It also helped us test similar AI approaches more safely in the future.
Understanding the feasibility of the idea

Our experiment demonstrated that natural language querying of graph data using LLMs is technically feasible, while also identifying important practical challenges around consistency, evaluation, and intent matching.

Understanding these limitations early helps reduce risk and provides a clearer foundation for future development. Building on this foundation could make complex graph data easier to interrogate for analysts and reduce repetitive query-writing requests for data scientists.
Building our own capability

The project also built reusable capability. We now have in-house tools and processes to generate synthetic datasets and evaluate LLM performance across both graph and non-graph use cases, simply by providing a schema and relevant inputs.

This has already accelerated experimentation across our AI teams. It will make future AI projects at BIST faster and cheaper to test before deciding whether to scale them. The lessons and evaluation methods developed through this work are also relevant across the public sector, where organisations face similar challenges in testing AI systems safely, reliably, and cost-effectively. Get in touch if you'd like to talk further about this.
What's next

The next step is understanding what it would take to move forward to a production-ready capability, if the approach proves reliable enough. This includes validating performance at scale, integrating with real environments and implementing appropriate guardrails and security controls.

We are also exploring ways to use AI to generate more realistic synthetic data. Rather than creating data that only follows the required structure, the aim is to generate data that better reflects real-world relationships and patterns. Over time, we hope this will make synthetic datasets more useful for testing and evaluating new AI applications.

Explainability is another focus area. We want to enable users not just to query data in plain English, but to receive results that are clearly explained and visualised. This would make graph data far more accessible to non-technical users.

Looking further ahead, there is potential to automate more parts of the experimentation process. For example, agents could support synthetic data generation, proof-of-concept creation, evaluation and quality assurance. This could reduce the time and effort required to evaluate new ideas. It could allow teams to test more concepts and focus their attention on higher-value review and decision-making activities. However, any such approach would require robust guardrails and multiple human checkpoints to ensure reliability and trust. These kinds of approaches benefit from collaboration between government and industry delivery partners, combining technical expertise with experience from a range of sectors.
Conclusion

This experiment showed that using AI to query graph databases in plain English is technically feasible. It has the potential to make complex network data more accessible to a wider range of users. However, the key lesson is that generating a valid query is not enough. The greater challenge is ensuring that the query accurately reflects the user's intent and consistently returns the answer they are actually looking for.

For data scientists, analysts and Digital and Data leaders considering similar approaches, this means placing as much emphasis on evaluation, governance and human review as on the AI technology itself. Success should be measured not only by whether a query runs, but by whether it produces trusted and meaningful results.

We would like to hear from others exploring AI-assisted querying, synthetic data generation or AI evaluation. How are you assessing whether AI-generated outputs reflect user intent? Where have you found human oversight remains essential?

title: What is an accelerator?
authors: Anna Goss, Deputy Director - Test, Learn and Grow, Public Sector Reform, Cabinet Office

content.content: In Autumn 2025 we started our accelerator projects: small, multidisciplinary teams working alongside places to design, test and scale solutions to complex public service challenges.

Rather than designing a solution centrally and rolling it out, an accelerator brings together people from central and local government to work side by side on a shared challenge. It will include people with a variety of skills such as service design, data, product, policy, analysis and delivery. This way of working means that solutions are designed for and specific to the needs of the communities we’re serving.

The accelerators are also trying to prove that test and learn is a legitimate and effective way of developing public policy close to the people we're serving. We are continuously evaluating, learning and adapting as we go. What we learn during the course of the accelerators directly shapes how we think about public service reform more broadly.

There's no fixed length to an accelerator: the timeline depends on the nature of the challenge and what the team and place partner learn along the way. What's consistent across every accelerator is the approach.
Starting with people, not assumptions

Every accelerator begins the same way: by listening, understanding and building relationships with places and our partners. Before anyone designs a solution, teams spend time understanding the problem from the perspective of the people living with it, whether that's residents, frontline practitioners, schools, the voluntary sector or local delivery partners. In most cases this means spending time in places to understand how communities experience their daily lives such as travelling to work or support services. It could also mean interviews with service users where they outline any issues they are facing, or sitting with local teams to understand how services currently work and where they fall short.
This stage matters because it's easy to wrongly assume you know what the problem is. Test and learn only works if you're honest about what you don't yet know.
Designing together

Once a team has a clearer picture of the problem, the next step is participatory design: bringing local partners, delivery staff, and often service users themselves into the room to collaborate and generate ideas together. The people who understand the local context and deliver services day to day help shape what gets tested. This is central to how we work.

Rather than committing to a large-scale rollout, accelerators test the riskiest assumptions first on a small scale. This might mean testing whether a particular group can be identified and reached before testing whether an intervention changes behaviour, or trying an idea with a handful of people before expanding it.

Starting small lowers risk. It means that if an assumption turns out to be wrong, the team finds out quickly and cheaply, rather than after investing months of effort and funding into something that doesn't work. It also means we can adapt fast when we learn something unexpected, rather than being locked into a plan that no longer fits the evidence.
Learning, always

We treat learning as continuous, not as a single phase with an endpoint. Every test, whether it succeeds or fails to produce the expected result, generates evidence that shapes what happens next. Teams regularly review findings, adjust their approach, and sometimes go back to first principles when something doesn't work as expected.

This means being honest about what doesn't go to plan. If a test doesn't produce the results we hoped for, that's not a failure of the programme, it's exactly how the model is supposed to work. We'd rather learn that something doesn't work on a small scale, quickly, than find out after a much larger rollout.

While each accelerator is rooted in a specific place, the aim is never just local improvement. Every accelerator is designed to generate insight that can inform national policy and practice and highlight wider, systemic barriers. This could include data-sharing arrangements, funding structures, or ways of working, that get in the way of good public service delivery everywhere.
That's why in Test, Learn, Grow we work hard to build feedback loops with central government departments, feeding what they learn locally back into national policy development and guidance.
Working as partners, not hierarchies

Underpinning all of this is a particular way of working. Accelerator teams don't sit above local partners directing activity, they work alongside them, as equals with different roles and expertise. Ideas, feedback and decisions flow in all directions.

This is important because accelerators are tackling challenges that are usually too complex for any single organisation or level of government to solve alone. Progress depends on genuine partnership between national and local government, alongside the wider ecosystem of place, which includes community organisations and citizens.
Nicola Bailey, Early Years and Family Hubs Service Lead in Manchester said:

“What Test, Learn and Grow does is create space for people to think differently and by turning up today the government is showing the level of commitment they’ve got to changing the outcomes for children and families and for us as a city..
“I always feel that my contribution is valued.”
What's next

Each of our accelerators is at a different stage and each is dealing with a genuinely difficult public service challenge. Over the coming months we'll share more from each place: what we're testing, what's working, and what isn't. We'll also introduce you to some of the people delivering this work on the ground in the places themselves.
If you want to follow along, you can subscribe for email notifications using the sign-up link, or join the Test, Learn and Grow community on LinkedIn.
